AWARD/JUDGMENT FACTUAL POSITION AND PLEADINGS 1.
This DAR was filed on 05/03/2019 by the Investigating Officer in the presence of the parties.
The DAR is related to a motor vehicular accident dated 10/12/2018 in which one Sh. Ram Ashre @ Ram Asre S/o Sh. Ram Lakhan (hereinafter referred to as "petitioner") sustained grievous injuries.

As per petitioner, on 10/12/2018 at about 03.30 P.M, he was standing at main door of his house at B-932,
Shastri Nagar, Delhi and suddenly on Motorcycle bearing registration number PANKAJ by PANKAJ SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.05.03 11:28:14 +0530 DL-6SN-7411 (hereinafter referred to as "offending vehicle") came from Shastri Nagar Metro Station in a very high speed, rash and negligent manner and hit the petitioner and due to which he received injuries.

It is further stated that landlord of the petitioner namely Sh. Har Narayan Maini s/o Sh. Vishwamitra Maini took the petitioner to Nazar Kunwar Surana Hospital, Gulabi Bagh, Delhi where the petitioner was medical treated and someone has made the PCR Call.

ISSUE NO.1 "Whether the petitioner Sh. Ram Ashre suffered injuries in an accident that took place on 10.12.2018 at about 15.30 involving Motorcycle bearing registration No. DL-6SN-7411 driven by Respondent No.1 rashly and negligently by the Respondent No. 1, owned by the Respondent No.2 and insured with the Respondent No.3?

It is well settled that the procedure followed for proceedings conducted by an accident tribunal is similar to that followed by a civil court and in civil matters the facts are required to be established by preponderance of probabilities only and not by strict rules of evidence or beyond reasonable doubts as are required in a criminal prosecution.

The burden of proof in a civil case is never as heavy as that is required in a criminal case, but in a claim petition under the Motor Vehicles Act, this burden is infact even lesser than that in a civil case.

Reference in this regard can be made to the propositions of law laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Bimla Devi and others Vs. Himachal Road Transport Corporation and others, reported in (2009) 13 SC 530, which were reiterated in the subsequent judgment in the case of Parmeshwari Vs. Amir Chand and others 2011 (1) SCR 1096 (Civil Appeal No.1082 of 2011) and also recently in another case Mangla Ram Vs. Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd. & Ors., 2018 Law Suit (SC) 303.
11.

16. In view of the above discussion, this Tribunal holds that the petitioner suffered injuries on his person on account of negligence and default of R-1 while driving the offending vehicle at the relevant time.
This issue thus stands decided against the respondents and in favour of the petitioner.
"Whether the petitioner is entitled for compensation?

If so, to what amount and from whom?
17.

As the issue no.1 has been proved in affirmative and in favour of the petitioner, the petitioner has become entitled to be compensated for the injuries suffered in the above accident, but the computation of compensation and liability to pay the same are required to be decided.
18. In terms of provisions contained in Section 168 of the MV Act the compensation which is to be awarded by this tribunal is required to be 'just'.
In the injury cases a claimant is entitled to two different kinds of compensations i.e. Pecuniary as well as non-pecuniary damages.

The "pecuniary damages" or PANKAJ Digitally signed by PANKAJ SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.05.03 11:28:50 +0530 special damages are those damages which are awarded and designed to make good the losses which are capable of being calculated in terms of money and the object of awarding these damages is to indemnify the claimant for the expenses which he had already incurred or is likely to incur in respect of the injuries suffered by her in the accident.
The "non-pecuniary" or general damages are those damages which are incapable of being assessed by arithmetical calculations.

The pecuniary or special damages generally include the expenses incurred by the claimant towards his treatment,
special diet, conveyance, cost of nursing/ attendant, loss of income/earning capacity etc. and the non- pecuniary damages generally include the compensation for the mental or physical shock, pain and sufferings, loss of amenities of life, marriage prospects and disfiguration etc.
The above categories falling under both the heads of compensation are not exhaustive in nature but only illustrative.

It is also necessary to state here that no amount of money or compensation can put the injured/claimant exactly in the same position or place where she was before the accident and an effort is to be made only to reasonably compensate her or to put her almost in the same place or position where he could have been if the alleged accident had not taken place and this compensation is to be assessed in a fair, reasonable and equitable manner.
The object of compensating her is also not to reward her or to make her rich in an unjust manner.
It is also well settled

that the 'just'
compensation to be awarded to the claimant has to be calculated objectively and it may involve some guess work in calculating the different amounts which the claimant may be entitled under the different heads of compensation.

Further, in case of PANKAJ PANKAJ SHARMA SHARMA Date:
2025.05.03 11:28:55 +0530 permanent disability, the assessment of compensation under the head of loss of future earning, would depend upon the effect and impact of such permanent disability on his earning capacity.

In light of the above legal propositions, the amount of compensation which can be considered to be 'just' in the opinion of this tribunal shall be as under:-
(i) Medical or Treatment Expenses 20.
The petitioner has placed on judicial file the original medical treatment records as well as medical bills vide Ex. PW-1/2 (colly).
As per the said documents, petitioner has incurred expenses to the tune of Rs.2,912/-.
In the absence of any contest to the said documents (placed on record by the petitioner), the petitioner is held entitled to an amount of Rs.2,912/- under this head.
(ii) Pain and Suffering 21.
As per medical documents, the petitioner has suffered grievous injuries
It is not possible to quantify the compensation admissible to petitioner for the shock, pain and sufferings etc. which he actually suffered because of the above PANKAJ PANKAJ SHARMA SHARMA
Date: 2025.05.03 11:29:01 +0530 injuries, but as stated above, an effort has to be made to compensate her for the same in a just and reasonable manner.

Hence, keeping in view the extent and nature of the injuries suffered by petitioner and duration of the treatment taken by him etc., an amount of Rs.50,000/- is being awarded to him towards pain and sufferings during the said period of his treatment and immobility.
Thus, she is awarded a total amount of Rs.50,000/- under this head.
(iii) Loss of actual earnings 22.

In his affidavit Ex. PW1/A, the petitioner claims that at the time of accident he was 44 years old and was doing the job of Head Worker in the Factory of Narain Enterprises and was earning Rs.26,000/- from the said job.
The medical records reflects that the petitioner suffered grievous injuries.

In view of the nature of the injuries sustained by the petitioner, it could be safely assumed that the petitioner could not have worked for about 03 months due to the injuries sustained in the accident.
In order to prove his income, the petitioner has filed his employment certificate issued by Narain Enterprises Ex. PW/1/4.
As per which, he was drawing salary of Rs. 26,000/- per month and accordingly same is considered for the purpose of computation of compensation.
As such, the petitioner is held entitled to a sum of Rs.78,000/- (Rs.26,000/- X 3).
The said sum is awarded to the petitioner under this head.

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
It is well settled that the procedure followed for proceedings conducted by an accident tribunal is similar to that followed by a civil court and in civil matters the facts are required to be established by preponderance of probabilities only and not by strict rules of evidence or beyond reasonable doubts as are required in a criminal prosecution.
The burden of proof in a civil case is never as heavy as that is required in a criminal case, but in a claim petition under the Motor Vehicles Act, this burden is infact even lesser than that in a civil case.
Reference in this regard can be made to the propositions of law laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Bimla Devi and others Vs. Himachal Road Transport Corporation and others, reported in (2009) 13 SC 530, which were reiterated in the subsequent judgment in the case of Parmeshwari Vs. Amir Chand and others 2011 (1) SCR 1096 (Civil Appeal No.1082 of 2011) and also recently in another case Mangla Ram Vs. Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd. & Ors., 2018 Law Suit (SC) 303.
11.
As such, it could be safely held that the oral testimony of PW-1 is reliable and trustworthy.
Therefore, an adverse inference on this aspect is also required to be drawn against the respondents in view of the law laid down in case of Cholamandalam M.S. General Insurance Company Ltd. Vs. Kamlesh, reported in 2009 (3) AD (Delhi) 310.
14.
In view of the above, it could be safely assumed that at the relevant time, R-1 was driving the offending vehicle at a wrong side in rash and negligent manner in a high speed and hit the motorcycle of the petitioner.
In the absence of any averment or evidence regarding any mechanical defect in the offending vehicle or any material depicting any negligent/sudden act or omission on the part of the petitioner, the only inference possible in the given facts and circumstances is that of neglect and default on the part of R-1 in driving the offending vehicle at the relevant time.
18. In terms of provisions contained in Section 168 of the MV Act the compensation which is to be awarded by this tribunal is required to be 'just'.
In the injury cases a claimant is entitled to two different kinds of compensations i.e. Pecuniary as well as non-pecuniary damages.
The "pecuniary damages" or PANKAJ Digitally signed by PANKAJ SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.05.03 11:28:50 +0530 special damages are those damages which are awarded and designed to make good the losses which are capable of being calculated in terms of money and the object of awarding these damages is to indemnify the claimant for the expenses which he had already incurred or is likely to incur in respect of the injuries suffered by her in the accident.
The "non-pecuniary" or general damages are those damages which are incapable of being assessed by arithmetical calculations.
The pecuniary or special damages generally include the expenses incurred by the claimant towards his treatment,
special diet, conveyance, cost of nursing/ attendant, loss of income/earning capacity etc. and the non- pecuniary damages generally include the compensation for the mental or physical shock, pain and sufferings, loss of amenities of life, marriage prospects and disfiguration etc.
The above categories falling under both the heads of compensation are not exhaustive in nature but only illustrative.
It is also necessary to state here that no amount of money or compensation can put the injured/claimant exactly in the same position or place where she was before the accident and an effort is to be made only to reasonably compensate her or to put her almost in the same place or position where he could have been if the alleged accident had not taken place and this compensation is to be assessed in a fair, reasonable and equitable manner.
The object of compensating her is also not to reward her or to make her rich in an unjust manner.
It is also well settled
that the 'just'
compensation to be awarded to the claimant has to be calculated objectively and it may involve some guess work in calculating the different amounts which the claimant may be entitled under the different heads of compensation.
subject like the judgment in the case of R.D. Hattangadi Vs. Pest Control (India) Pvt. Ltd., AIR 1995 SC 755, Arvind Kumar Mishra Vs. New India Assurance Company Limited, (2010) 10 SCC 254 and Raj Kumar Vs. Ajay Kumar & Anr., (2011) 1 SCC 343.
19.
The petitioner has placed on judicial file the original medical treatment records as well as medical bills vide Ex. PW-1/2 (colly).
As per medical documents, the petitioner has suffered grievous injuries
It is not possible to quantify the compensation admissible to petitioner for the shock, pain and sufferings etc. which he actually suffered because of the above PANKAJ PANKAJ SHARMA SHARMA
Nor have they bothered to place any valid and effective driving licence of R-1 on record.
Accordingly, it could be safely assumed that R-1 was driving the offending vehicle without any valid and effective driving licence.
This entitles R-3 to be granted recovery rights against R-2 only since R-1 was minor at the relevant time.
